title: Ketchaponack
summary: Ketchaponack is a Southampton placename for a neck of land in the Westhampton Beach area, in the western part of Southampton town on Quantuck Creek near the historic West Hampton post office area.
address_label: General Ketchaponack / Quantuck Creek area, Westhampton Beach, New York
introduction_content: Ketchaponack was a named neck in the Westhampton landscape of salt marsh, freshwater and bay access. Its history includes reserved meadow as well as the later colonial division of the surrounding land. Tooker, pp. 80–81
history_content:
A 1663 record cited by Tooker mentions five acres of salt marsh reserved at Ketchaponack. In the town’s 1686 division, Aspatuck and Monabaugs swamp helped locate the neck. These descriptions show why a single village-center point cannot stand for all the resources and boundaries attached to the name. Tooker, pp. 80–81

The 1686 town-book descriptions can be read together to compare the neighboring necks, waterways and crossings. Southampton town records, vol. II, printed pp. 113–114
translation_content:
Recorded spellings include Ketcheponack, Catchponack, Catchaponack, Ketchabonack, Ketchabonnack, and Catcheboneck. Potunk appears in related Westhampton source context but is also maintained as its own nearby placename record. The name has been connected with large edible roots or yellow water lily, though that interpretation should be checked against the original source.

Why Place Names Matter

“Names also embody a sense of belonging to a place, coexistence with the natural world and the longstanding relationship between a People and their place; they anchor the past to the present.”

— Bob Joseph, The Relationship Between Indigenous Peoples and Place Names (2016), Article paragraph 12

Ketchaponack ties a Native placename to a named neck, creek, marsh, and later town-record landscape. Indigenous place names remained in local boundary descriptions, land records, and neighborhood memory.

Tooker reports competing interpretations involving large roots, including different proposed wetland plants and groundnuts. Those proposals should not be treated as a verified identification of a plant, a community-confirmed translation, or evidence that a species can be harvested here. Tooker, pp. 80–81
land_loss_content: Ketchaponack ties a Native placename to a named neck, creek, marsh, and later town-record landscape. Indigenous place names remained in local boundary descriptions, land records, and neighborhood memory.
whereintheworld_content: The pin gives a broad Westhampton reference. The 1686 town record places Catchaponack between Aspatuck on the east and Monabaugs swamp on the west. The swamp’s full historical extent has not been securely matched to modern features, so the pin does not claim the exact limits of the neck. Tooker, pp. 80–81
